paragraphs: “Gentlemen,” he began, still as agitated as before, “I want to make a full confession: that money was _my own_.” The lawyers’ faces fell. This was nothing like what they had expected.
“What do you mean?” stammered Nikolay Parfenovitch. “At five o’clock on that same day, by your own confession—”

“Damn five o’clock that day and my own confession! That has nothing to do with it now! That money was my own, my own, that is, stolen by me ... not mine, I mean, but stolen by me, and it was fifteen hundred roubles, and I had it on me all the time, all the time ...”
“But where did you get it?”

“I took it off my neck, gentlemen, off this very neck ... it was here, around my neck, sewn up in a rag. I’d been wearing it a long time, a month now, since I hung it round my neck ... to my shame and disgrace!”
“And from whom did you ... appropriate it?”
“You mean ‘steal it’? Say it plainly now. Yes, I consider that I as good as stole it, but if you prefer, I ‘appropriated it.’ I consider that I stole it. And last night I stole it for good.”
“Last night? But you said it’s a month since you ... obtained it?...”

“Yes. But not from my father. Not from my father, don’t worry. I didn’t steal it from my father but from her. Let me tell it without interruptions. It’s hard enough, you know. You see, a month ago Katerina Ivanovna, who used to be my betrothed, sent for me. Do you know her?”
“Yes, of course.”
“I know you know her. She’s a noble creature, the noblest of the noble. But she’s hated me for ever so long, oh, ever so long ... and she had good reason to hate me, good reason!”
“Katerina Ivanovna!” Nikolay Parfenovitch exclaimed in amazement. The prosecutor stared too.

“Oh, don’t take her name in vain! I’m a scoundrel to drag her into this. Yes, I’ve seen that she hated me ... for a long while.... From the very first, even that evening at my lodging ... but enough, enough. You’re not fit even to know about that. There’s no need of it at all.... I only need to tell you that a month ago she sent for me and gave me three thousand roubles to send off to her sister and another relation in Moscow (as though she couldn’t have sent it herself!) and I ... it was just at that fatal moment in my life when I ... well, in short, when I’d just fallen in love with another woman, with her, she’s sitting downstairs now, Grushenka. I carried her off here to Mokroe then, and in two days I wasted half of that damned three thousand, but the other half I kept on me. Well, I kept that other half, that fifteen hundred, like a locket round my neck, but yesterday I undid it and spent it. What’s left of it, eight hundred roubles, is in your hands now, Nikolay Parfenovitch. That’s the change from the fifteen hundred I had yesterday.”
“Excuse me. How is that? When you were here a month ago you spent three thousand, not fifteen hundred. Everybody knows that.”
“Who knows it? Who counted the money? Did I let anyone count it?”
“But you told everyone yourself that you’d spent exactly three thousand.”

“It’s true, I did. I told the whole town so, and the whole town repeated it. And here at Mokroe, too, everyone reckoned it was three thousand. Yet I didn’t spend three thousand, but fifteen hundred. And the other fifteen hundred I sewed into a little bag. That’s how it was, gentlemen. That’s where I got that money yesterday....”
“This is almost miraculous,” murmured Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“Allow me to ask,” the prosecutor remarked at last, “whether you had told anyone at all about this before—that is, that you had fifteen hundred left on you a month ago?”
“I told no one.”
“That’s strange. Do you mean absolutely no one?”
“Absolutely no one. No one and nobody.”

“What was your reason for this reticence? What was your motive for making such a secret of it? To put it more precisely: you have finally told us your secret, which you call so ‘disgraceful,’ though in reality—that is, of course, comparatively speaking—this action, that is, the appropriation of three thousand roubles belonging to someone else, and, of course, only temporarily, is in my view at least merely an act of the greatest recklessness, and not so disgraceful, when one takes your character into consideration.... Even granting that it was a highly discreditable action, still, discreditable is not ‘disgraceful.’... Many people have already guessed, during this last month, about the three thousand of Katerina Ivanovna’s that you have spent, and I heard the story myself, quite apart from your confession.... Mihail Makarovitch, for instance, had heard it too, so that it was hardly a story at all, but the gossip of the whole town. There are indications, too, if I am not mistaken, that you confessed this yourself to someone, I mean that the money was Katerina Ivanovna’s. And so it is extremely surprising to me that until now, that is, up to this moment, you have made such an extraordinary secret of the fifteen hundred you say you put aside, and seem to connect a feeling of positive horror with that secret.... It is not easy to believe that confessing such a secret could cost you such distress.... You cried out, just now, that Siberia would be better than confessing it ...”

The prosecutor stopped speaking. He was irritated. He did not hide his annoyance, which was almost anger, and let out all his built-up spleen, disjointedly and incoherently, without choosing his words.
“It’s not the fifteen hundred that’s the disgrace, but that I set it apart from the rest of the three thousand,” said Mitya firmly.

“Why?” the prosecutor smiled irritably. “What is disgraceful, in your view, about having set aside half of the three thousand that you had discreditably, or if you prefer, ‘disgracefully,’ appropriated? Your taking the three thousand matters more than what you did with it. And by the way, why did you do that—why did you set that half apart, for what purpose, to what end? Can you explain that to us?”

“Oh, gentlemen, the purpose is the whole point!” cried Mitya. “I put it aside because I was vile, that is, because I was calculating, and to be calculating in such a case is vile ... and that vileness has been going on for a whole month.”
“It’s incomprehensible.”

“I’m amazed at you. But I’ll make it clearer. Perhaps it really is incomprehensible. You see, listen to what I say. Suppose I appropriate three thousand entrusted to my honor, and I spend it on a spree, say I spend all of it, and next morning I go to her and say, ‘Katya, I’ve done wrong, I’ve squandered your three thousand.’ Well, is that right? No, it’s not right—it’s dishonest and cowardly. I’m a beast, with no more self-control than a beast, that’s so, isn’t it? But still I’m not a thief? Not a downright thief, you’ll admit! I squandered it, but I didn’t steal it. Now a second, somewhat more favorable alternative: follow me carefully, or I may get confused again—my head’s spinning—and so, the second alternative: I spend only fifteen hundred of the three thousand here, that is, only half. Next day I go and take that half to her: ‘Katya, take this fifteen hundred from me. I’m a low beast and an untrustworthy scoundrel, for I’ve wasted half the money, and I’ll waste this too, so keep me from temptation!’ Well, what about that alternative? I’d be a beast and a scoundrel, and whatever you like; but not a thief, not altogether a thief, or I wouldn’t have brought back what was left, but would have kept that too. She would see at once that since I brought back half, I would pay back what I’d spent, that I would never give up trying to, that I would work to get it and pay it back. So in that case I’d be a scoundrel, but not a thief, say what you like, not a thief!”
“I admit that there is a certain distinction,” said the prosecutor, with a cold smile. “But it’s strange that you see such a vital difference.”

“Yes, I see a vital difference! Every man may be a scoundrel, and perhaps every man is a scoundrel, but not everyone can be a thief. It takes an arch-scoundrel to be that. Oh, of course, I don’t know how to make these fine distinctions ... but a thief is lower than a scoundrel, that’s my conviction. Listen, I carry the money on me a whole month, I may make up my mind to give it back tomorrow, and I’m a scoundrel no longer, but I can’t make up my mind, you see, though I’m making it up every day, and every day spurring myself on to do it, and yet for a whole month I can’t bring myself to it, you see. Is that right in your opinion, is that right?”

“Certainly, that’s not right, that I can quite understand, and I don’t dispute it,” answered the prosecutor with reserve. “And let us drop all discussion of these subtleties and distinctions and, if you would be so kind, get back to the point. And the point is that you still have not told us—we have asked you, after all—why, in the first place, you halved the money, squandering one half and hiding the other. For what purpose exactly did you hide it? What did you mean to do with that fifteen hundred? I insist on that question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, of course!” cried Mitya, striking himself on the forehead. “Forgive me, I’m wearing you out and not explaining the main point, or you’d understand in a minute, for it’s just the motive that’s the disgrace! You see, it was all to do with the old man, my dead father. He was always pestering Agrafena Alexandrovna, and I was jealous. I thought then that she was hesitating between me and him. So every day I kept thinking, suppose she were to make up her mind all of a sudden, suppose she were to stop tormenting me and say to me, ‘I love you, not him; take me to the other end of the world.’ And I had only forty kopecks; how could I take her away, what could I do? Why, I’d be lost. You see, I didn’t know her then, I didn’t understand her. I thought she wanted money and wouldn’t forgive my poverty. And so I fiendishly counted out half of that three thousand and sewed it up, counting on it—sewed it up before I was drunk, and after I’d sewn it up, I went off to get drunk on the rest. Yes, that was base. Do you understand now?”
Both the lawyers laughed out loud.
“I’d have called it sensible and moral of you not to have squandered it all,” chuckled Nikolay Parfenovitch, “for after all, what does it amount to?”

“It amounts to this, that I stole it! Oh, God, you horrify me by not understanding! Every day that I had that fifteen hundred sewn up round my neck, every day and every hour I said to myself, ‘You’re a thief! You’re a thief!’ Yes, that’s why I’ve been so savage all this month, that’s why I fought in the tavern, that’s why I attacked my father: it was because I felt I was a thief. I couldn’t make up my mind, I didn’t dare even to tell Alyosha, my brother, about that fifteen hundred: I felt I was such a scoundrel and such a pickpocket. But, you know, while I carried it I also said to myself every hour: ‘No, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you may yet not be a thief.’ Why? Because I might go next day and pay back that fifteen hundred to Katya. And only yesterday I made up my mind to tear my amulet off my neck, on my way from Fenya’s to Perhotin. Until that moment I hadn’t been able to bring myself to it. And it was only when I tore it off that I became a downright thief, a thief and a dishonest man for the rest of my life. Why? Because with that I destroyed, too, my dream of going to Katya and saying, ‘I’m a scoundrel, but not a thief!’ Do you understand now? Do you understand?”
“What made you decide to do it yesterday?” Nikolay Parfenovitch interrupted.

“Why? It’s absurd to ask. Because I had condemned myself to die at five o’clock this morning, here, at dawn. I thought it made no difference whether I died a thief or a man of honor. But I see it’s not so; it turns out that it does make a difference. Believe me, gentlemen, what has tortured me most during this night has not been the thought that I’d killed the old servant, or that I was in danger of Siberia just when my love was being rewarded and Heaven was open to me again. Oh, that did torture me, but not in the same way: not so much as the damned consciousness that I had torn that damned money off my breast at last and spent it, and had become a downright thief! Oh, gentlemen, I tell you again, with a bleeding heart, I have learned a great deal this night. I have learned that it’s not only impossible to live a scoundrel, but impossible to die a scoundrel.... No, gentlemen, one must die honest....”
Mitya was pale. His face looked haggard and exhausted, though he was intensely excited.

“I am beginning to understand you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said slowly, in a soft and almost compassionate tone. “But all this, if you’ll excuse my saying so, is in my opinion a matter of nerves ... your overwrought nerves, that’s what it is. And why, for instance, should you not have spared yourself such misery for almost a month, by going and returning that fifteen hundred to the lady who had entrusted it to you? And why could you not have explained things to her? In view of your position, which you describe as so awful, why could you not have had recourse to the plan that would so naturally occur to one—that is, after honorably confessing your errors to her, why could you not have asked her to lend you the sum you needed for your expenses? With her generous heart she would certainly not have refused you in your distress, especially if you had offered some guarantee, or even the security you offered to the merchant Samsonov and to Madame Hohlakov. I suppose you still regard that security as of value?”
